background.definition:
Tinea capitis and tinea barbae are fungal infections of the hair follicles and surrounding skin, primarily caused by dermatophyic fungi of the genera Trichophyton and Microsporum.
These fungi invade skin, hair, and other keratinized tissues and require keratin to grow. Tinea capitis specifically involves infection of the scalp region and tinea barbae is infection of the hair-bearing regions of the face and neck (beard distribution).

list.listitem: Tinea capitis is primarily a disease of children between the ages of 3 and 7 years. In the U.S., 3% to 8% of children are affected, with a carriage rate of 34% among household contacts. In the U.K., 2.5% of school-age children are affected, with a carriage rate of 12% to 47%.

Tinea barbae is primarily a disease of adolescent boys and adult men. Prevalence has decreased as single-use razors have become more widespread. It remains more common in tropical, humid climates and in rural areas where cattle are present and spread it to humans.
Tinea capitis is the most common pediatric dermatophyte infection.
Tinea barbae is a much more rare dermatophyte infection.
Trichophyton tonsurans: United States, Central America, and Western Europe (>90% cases in these areas).
Microsporum canis and M. audouinii: South America, Southern and Central Europe, Africa, and Middle East.
Trichophyton violaceum and Trichophyton soudanense: Primarily Africa, but becoming more common in the United States.
Most infections are zoophilic (spread from infected animals) or anthropophilic (spread from infected humans).

Zoophilic fungi are the predominant cause of tinea barbae, so have a high index of suspicion in adolescent boys and men who work with pets, domestic animals, or have other potential exposures.
Trichophyton mentagrophytes and Trichophyton verrucosum are the most common zoophilic causes
Trichophyton rubrum and Trichophyton violaceum are common anthropophilic causes
Men with diabetes, on immunosuppressant therapy, or with trauma to their skin are also more at risk of infection.
Sometimes, infection can spread from onychomycosis or tinea pedis.
Endothrix infections (primarily Trichophyton) invade and grow within the hair shaft without damage to the cuticle.
Ectothrix infections (primarily Microsporum) are defined by fungi adhering to and growing in the sheath around the hair shaft, destroying the cuticle.

In children suspected of tinea capitis, those with adenopathy had a high likelihood of positive fungal culture (LR+ 7.5). Fungal culture is rarely positive if the child lacks alopecia and adenopathy. B

list.listitem: Typical clinical appearance is of alopecia with single or multiple patches of hair loss (LR 3.3). Presentation can range from asymptomatic carrier states to non-inflammatory areas of hair loss to inflammatory, pustular patches of hair loss.

Symptomatic patients often have cervical lymphadenopathy (LR 7.5). Pruritis (LR 1.4) and scaling (LR 1.1) occur less frequently. Fungal culture is rarely positive in the child lacking alopecia and adenopathy.
Tinea capitis is frequently associated with numerous broken-off hairs just above the skin surface giving a "black dot" appearance. The dots will be color of patient's hair.
Patients may also have areas with marked scaling, referred to as "grey patch." Alternatively, patients may have areas of alopecia with boggy edema called kerion secondary to aggressive inflammation.
Similar to tinea capitis, tinea barbae also presents as inflammatory (typically caused by zoophilic infections) or noninflammatory (typically caused by anthropophilic infections).16, 24, 27
Inflammatory tinea barbae presents as one or multiple kerions.16, 27
Noninflammatory tinea barbae presents as pustular and papular erythematous plaques.16, 27

Examination with Wood's lamp has been used historically, but only Microsporum species (Ectothrix-fungi coating hair) fluoresce yellow-green. This currently represents less than 10% of tinea infections in the United States.

Microscopic analysis of plucked hairs placed in 10% to 30% KOH and humidified for 30 minutes will frequently show hyphae and spores under 40x magnification. However, false negatives are relatively common and histopathology is rarely used to make the diagnosis.

Culture of hairs or skin scraping (gathered using sterile toothbrush, swab, or gauze) on appropriate media should be considered, especially if patients do not respond to initial therapy. The culture may show growth in 7 to 10 days, but it requires 30 days of no growth to be negative. A PCR test has been developed but is not widely available.

For tinea capitis, the typical appearance is single or multiple patches of hair loss, frequently associated "black dot" appearance, and cervical lymphadenopathy, possible inflammation, scaling, pustules, and itching.

Tinea barbae begins in areas of facial hair on the face and neck, most commonly with loose hairs, sometimes scarred patches of hair loss, inflammatory draining pustular nodules, and abscesses or kerions.
Examination with Wood's lamp only fluoresces with Microsporum species (cause of <10% US infections), so this is relatively unhelpful.

Microscopic analysis of plucked hairs may reveal fungi within the hair shaft. Although false negatives are common, microscopic examination is the best diagnostic test to identify the fungal elements of tinea barbae.
Consider culture of hairs or skin scraping on appropriate media (mycological diagnosis), especially if initial therapy is unsuccessful.
Systemic therapy is required; topical is not sufficient. A

Consider griseofulvin for 6 to 8 weeks (20-25 mg/kg/d for children, 500 mg/d for adults). Alternatively, consider terbinafine for 4 weeks in children older than 4 years (62.5 mg/d <20 kg, 125 mg/d if 20-40 kg, or 250 mg/d if >40 kg. A
Topical therapy with selenium sulfide, ciclopirox, or povidine-iodine shampoo may help increase eradication rates but alone is not sufficient therapy. B
See for summary of medication options for the treatment of tinea capitis and barbae.

Systemic antifungal therapy is required for tinea capitis and tinea barbae. Topical therapy does not adequately reach the root of hair follicles. Lack of mycologic cure may necessitate longer courses of all medications. Newer oral antifungals show equal efficacy with shorter courses but at increased costs. Not all are approved against tinea capitis in all countries.

A 2 to 4 week course of terbinafine was shown as effective as 6 to 8 weeks of griseofulvin. Terbinafine is Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved for treatment of tinea capitis in children older than 4 years.Terbinafine is not approved by the FDA for the specific treatment of tinea capitis in adults.

Griseofulvin and terbinafine are both effective and well tolerated in the treatment of tinea capitis, although griseofulvin is cheaper. In one RCT, children were randomized to either griseofulvin for 8 weeks or terbinafine for 4 weeks. Parents were also advised to use ketoconazole shampoo. All but one was culture negative at the end of 8 weeks. The single treatment failure was treated with terbinafine initially and was still culture positive after 8 weeks of griseofulvin. Another study showed cure rates of 92% with griseofulvin for 6 weeks compared to 94% with terbinafine, 86% with itraconazole, and 84% with fluconazole (each for 2-3 weeks).

Another meta-analysis found seven comparative studies, showing that griseofulvin is better for Microsporum and terbinafine for Trichophyton species. This approach of preferring griseofulvin for Microsporum tinea capitis has been endorsed by European guidelines and Cochrane review.

Fluconazole 6 mg/kg/d for 3 to 6 weeks is an alternative choice for the treatment of tinea capitis.1,
Fluconazole is not FDA-approved for this indication.
Itraconazole 5mg/kg/d for 3 to 6 weeks is an alternative choice for the treatment of tinea capitis.1, 18, 20, 22 Itraconazole is not FDA-approved for this indication.

Topical therapy is only useful along with appropriate oral therapy (ie, as an adjunctive therapy). Selenium sulfide shampoo increases rate of eradication when used with oral therapy. Povidine-iodine shampoo twice weekly reduces viable spore carriage. Ciclopirox shampoo 1% had similar efficacy compared to selenium sulfide 1% as adjunctive therapy.
Do not incise a kerion. It is not an abscess; it is an inflammatory reaction to the dermatophyte.
If disease is identified in pets, patient may benefit from veterinary referral and treatment of pet.
If other children are in the home, avoid sharing hair care items.
Cure rates with oral therapy are similar between griseofulvlin 6-8 weeks and terbinafine for 4 weeks. A
Consider liver function tests at baseline and again if prolonged course of therapy. C
